title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to the core use case of issue tracking and project planning, and the key reason being the desire for more control over their data and costs. Teams looking for a self-hosted solution with a free, open-source license may find this comparison particularly useful.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira has a per-user monthly fee, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to have full control over their data, whereas Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, whereas Jira offers a more straightforward, cloud-based solution.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large, complex projects, while Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration difference: Jira has a wider range of integrations with third-party tools, including many popular DevOps and ITSM solutions, whereas Plane has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Scalable and suitable for large, complex projects
* User-friendly interface and easy to set up
* Robust reporting and analytics capabilities
* Good customer support
**Plane:**
* Free and self-hosted, with full control over data
* Customizable and flexible
* Suitable for smaller to medium-sized teams
* Open-source and community-driven
* Limited costs, aside from server maintenance

## When to Choose Each
Jira is the better choice for large, complex projects that require a wide range of integrations and a scalable solution. It is also suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use and are willing to pay a premium for a cloud-based solution. On the other hand, Plane is the better choice for smaller to medium-sized teams that value control over their data and are looking for a cost-effective, self-hosted solution. Teams with technical expertise and a desire for customization may also prefer Plane.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Use a third-party import tool, such as the Plane Importer, to migrate your data to Plane.
3. Configure your Plane instance to match your Jira workflow and settings.
4. Test your Plane instance to ensure that all data and functionality have been successfully migrated.
5. Train your team on the new Plane system and retire your Jira instance.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of more established project management tools like Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Plane's reporting and analytics capabilities are not yet as robust as Jira's. However, for teams that value control over their data and are looking for a cost-effective, self-hosted solution, Plane is definitely worth considering, and we recommend switching to Plane if you are a small to medium-sized team with simple project management needs and a technical team that can handle the setup and maintenance.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need advanced reporting and analytics capabilities
* Teams with technical expertise that can handle the setup and maintenance of a self-hosted solution
* Organizations with limited budgets that are looking for a cost-effective project management solution
* Teams that value control over their data and are willing to sacrifice some features and polish for a free, open-source solution
* Teams with simple project management needs that do not require a wide range of integrations with third-party tools

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted, with no per-user fees.
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format and use a third-party import tool to migrate it to Plane.
### Is Plane suitable for large, complex projects?
No, Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams and projects.
### Does Plane have a user-friendly interface?
Plane's interface is not as polished as Jira's, but it is still relatively easy to use, especially for teams with technical expertise.
### Are there any limitations to Plane's reporting and analytics capabilities?
Yes, Plane's reporting and analytics capabilities are not yet as robust as Jira's, but the community is actively working on improving them.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: WeKan is a free, self-hosted alternative to Trello. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are cloud storage solutions that enable individuals and teams to store, share, and collaborate on files. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams seeking a reliable and secure cloud storage solution, particularly those considering switching from a proprietary service like Dropbox to a self-hosted alternative like Nextcloud. The core use case for both tools is file storage and sharing, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Dropbox charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Nextcloud allows users to maintain full ownership and control over their data, whereas Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* Setup complexity: Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, especially for self-hosting, compared to Dropbox's user-friendly interface.
* Scalability: Nextcloud can be more scalable than Dropbox, especially for large teams or organizations, since it can be self-hosted on custom infrastructure.
* Integration with calendar: Nextcloud has a built-in calendar app that integrates seamlessly with its cloud storage, whereas Dropbox relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $499.50-$829/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $1,998-$3,316/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Robust security features
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data ownership and storage
**Nextcloud:**
* Self-hosting option for full control over data
* High scalability and customization
* Integrated calendar and contact apps
* Free to use with self-hosting
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

## When to Choose Each
Dropbox is a good choice for small teams or individuals who prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data. It's also a good option for those who need a wide range of integrations with third-party apps. On the other hand, Nextcloud is suitable for larger teams or organizations that require high scalability, customization, and control over their data. It's also a good choice for those who value self-hosting and don't mind the added complexity.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Dropbox data in ZIP format using the Dropbox website or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Nextcloud instance on your own server or use a pre-configured appliance.
3. Use the Nextcloud web interface to import your exported Dropbox data.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as user accounts and permissions.
5. Test your Nextcloud instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready solution for most users, offering a high degree of customization and control over data. However, it's essential to note that Nextcloud's self-hosting requirement can be a significant technical limitation for some users, particularly those without experience in server administration. For teams and individuals who value control over their data and are willing to invest time in setup and maintenance, Nextcloud is a clear recommendation.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't require a wide range of integrations and value self-hosting
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) who need high scalability and customization
* Large organizations (over 50 users) that require full control over their data and storage
* Individuals who prioritize data ownership and security
* Teams that don't need a user-friendly interface and are comfortable with technical complexity

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud for free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting, but you'll need to cover the cost of server infrastructure and maintenance.
### Is Nextcloud more secure than Dropbox?
Nextcloud offers similar security features to Dropbox, but its self-hosting option provides an additional layer of control and security.
### Can I integrate Nextcloud with my existing calendar app?
Yes, Nextcloud has a built-in calendar app, and you can also integrate it with other calendar apps using third-party plugins.
### How long does it take to set up Nextcloud?
The setup time for Nextcloud varies depending on your technical expertise and the complexity of your setup, but it can take anywhere from a few hours to several days.
### Is Nextcloud compatible with all file types?
Nextcloud supports most common file types, but it may not be compatible with certain proprietary or specialized file formats.

# Google Workspace vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Google Workspace and Nextcloud are two popular productivity and collaboration platforms that cater to different needs and use cases. The core use case for both tools is to provide a unified platform for teams to collaborate and work efficiently, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Google Workspace charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free and self-hosted.
* Data Ownership: Google Workspace stores data on its servers, while Nextcloud allows users to host their data on their own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Google Workspace is generally easier to set up, while Nextcloud requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: Google Workspace is highly scalable, while Nextcloud's scalability depends on the user's server infrastructure.
* Integration: Google Workspace integrates seamlessly with other Google apps, while Nextcloud offers integration with a range of third-party apps, including OnlyOffice for document editing.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $300-$900/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,200-$3,600/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Google Workspace:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Highly scalable and reliable
* Integrates seamlessly with other Google apps
* Offers a range of collaboration features
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Nextcloud:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Offers more control over data storage and security
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Integrates with a range of third-party apps
* Can be more complex to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Google Workspace is a good choice for teams that require a highly scalable and reliable platform with seamless integration with other Google apps. It is ideal for large teams with simple collaboration needs and a budget to support the monthly fees. On the other hand, Nextcloud is a good choice for teams that require more control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources in setting up and maintaining their own servers. It is ideal for small to medium-sized teams with complex collaboration needs and a limited budget.

## Migration Path
1. Export data from Google Workspace using the Google Takeout tool, which exports data in a variety of formats, including CSV and JSON.
2. Set up a Nextcloud server, either on-premises or with a cloud provider.
3. Use the Nextcloud Import tool to import the exported data into Nextcloud.
4. Configure Nextcloud to meet the team's specific needs, including setting up user accounts and permissions.
5. Test the migration to ensure that all data has been transferred correctly and that the team can collaborate effectively using Nextcloud.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a range of features and a high degree of customizability. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Nextcloud's scalability depends on the user's server infrastructure, which can be a challenge for large teams. Overall, we recommend Nextcloud for teams that require more control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources in setting up and maintaining their own servers.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that require a free or low-cost collaboration platform and do not need advanced features like Google Drive.

* Teams that require more control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources in setting up and maintaining their own servers, and do not need advanced security features like two-factor authentication.
* Teams with limited IT resources and a simple collaboration needs, and do not require advanced customization options.
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and security, and are willing to invest time and resources in setting up and maintaining their own servers, and do not need advanced integration with third-party apps.

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud with my existing Google account?
No, Nextcloud requires a separate user account and authentication system. However, you can use Nextcloud with your existing Google account as an external authentication source.
### Is Nextcloud free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free and open-source, but you will need to pay for your own server infrastructure and maintenance.
### Can I integrate Nextcloud with other Google apps?
Yes, Nextcloud offers integration with a range of third-party apps, including Google Drive and Google Calendar, but it may require additional setup and configuration.

Yes, Nextcloud offers a range of security features, including encryption and two-factor authentication, but it is up to the user to configure and maintain these features.
